notes: Article 8 removal JR; Sullivan J applied Huang proportionality and refused permission on non-exceptional facts.

enrichment.short_title: Nakalanzi: Article 8 proportionality and removal to Uganda
key_facts: The claimant, a failed Ugandan asylum seeker, challenged removal directions dated 20 August 2004.
She initially claimed arrival in April 2003 after alleged family killings in Uganda, but later asserted arrival in January 2003 and a family life with Mr Kironde and their son Dias.
The adjudicator and Immigration Appeal Tribunal rejected her Article 8 claim based on ties with her aunt; the Kironde relationship was raised only after removal directions were issued.
The Secretary of State maintained refusal, contending any interference was proportionate and temporary pending entry clearance from Kampala.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of removal directions after permission was granted, following adjournment and further evidence directions.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; even assuming facts in the claimant's favour, the case was not truly exceptional under Huang and removal was not disproportionate.
enrichment.ratio: Following Huang, Article 8 may justify remaining outside the Immigration Rules only in truly exceptional cases; a brief, late-formed family life entered when immigration status was precarious, coupled with inconsistent asylum history, does not meet that threshold and cannot prevent return for entry clearance.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant's family life with Mr Kironde made removal disproportionate under Article 8(2)
Application of Huang on the 'truly exceptional' test outside the Immigration Rules
Whether temporary separation pending entry clearance from Uganda rendered removal disproportionate
Relevance of the claimant's inconsistent immigration and asylum history to proportionality
linked_authorities: Huang v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 105
R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27

notes: Representative action against unincorporated club members; judgment debt enforceable but not costs per Moon v Atherton.

enrichment.short_title: Howells v Dominion: enforcing insurance judgment against club members
key_facts: Hemel Hempstead Football and Sports Club, an unincorporated members' club, sued Dominion Insurance after a 1992 fire; representative proceedings were brought by the chairman and secretary.
Deputy Judge Fernyhough entered judgment for Dominion on the claim and counterclaim for return of interim payments totalling over £75,000 plus assessed costs.
Dominion sought CPR 19.6(4) permission to enforce against 32 named members; Master Foster set aside permission on lack of authority to litigate and Moon v Atherton on costs.
All club members were parties to the insurance contract through the secretary; the committee had authority to contract but not, the Master held, to expose members to litigation risk.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a master's decision on whether judgment and a costs certificate could be enforced against individual members of an unincorporated association in representative proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the judgment debt: individual members could be liable and enforcement permission should be reconsidered; appeal dismissed on costs, represented members remain not individually liable for costs.
enrichment.ratio: In representative proceedings under CPR 19.6, represented members need not authorise litigation to be bound by the result; where all members were insured under the contract, the judgment debt is enforceable against them individually, but represented non-parties remain not liable for costs following Moon v Atherton.
legal_issues: Whether club members authorised representative litigation and could resist enforcement
Whether individual members were personally liable on the insurance contract judgment
Whether CPR 19.6(4)(b) permits enforcement of costs against represented non-parties
Distinction between authority to contract and authority to litigate in unincorporated associations

notes: Planning permission construction preliminary issue; 1999 cooking plant permission limited to agricultural pig-farm use.

enrichment.short_title: Mid Suffolk v Clarke: scope of cooking plant planning permission
key_facts: Mid Suffolk District Council sought a section 187B injunction to stop industrial rendering and waste processing at Rookery Farm, Drinkstone.
Planning permission 882/98 granted in February 1999 authorised demolition of a piggery and erection of a replacement cooking plant with odour controls during nuisance litigation.
After foot-and-mouth ended swill feeding, the defendant used the plant for avian offal rendering; a 2001 change-of-use application was refused and an appeal dismissed.
The defendant argued the permission summary alone authorised unrestricted industrial use of the cooking plant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue trial on the proper construction and scope of planning permission 882/98 in injunction proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issue decided for the council; permission was for a replacement cooking plant as part of continuing agricultural pig farming, not unrestricted industrial rendering.
enrichment.ratio: Planning permission must be construed from the operative grant and incorporated application documents, not the brief development description alone; here conditions and supporting papers showed the cooking plant was authorised only for feed and by-products connected with pig farming on the site.
legal_issues: Whether planning permission 882/98 authorised industrial rendering use of the cooking plant
Proper construction of planning permissions and use of extrinsic application materials
Whether a material change of use from agricultural to industrial use had occurred
Effect of conditions including condition 7 on cooked feed and by-products

notes: Bail refusal JR; section 29(3) excluded but Wednesbury challenge failed on breach of bail conditions.

enrichment.short_title: Shergill v Harrow Crown Court: judicial review of bail refusal
key_facts: The claimant, aged 22, was charged with assault occasioning ABH on a local authority support worker following an altercation at his girlfriend's address.
He was granted conditional bail by magistrates and extended at plea and directions, including not to contact the co-defendant or enter Harrow.
On 6 March he breached bail by visiting his girlfriend in Harrow; HHJ Black refused bail on 10 March with no recorded reasons beyond fear of further offences and breach.
Harrow Crown Court did not record oral reasons for bail refusals, relying on a standard printed form.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review after urgent vacation permission to quash a Crown Court bail refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; section 29(3) did not bar review but the refusal was within Wednesbury bounds given bail breaches and risk of further offences.
enrichment.ratio: Decisions on bail before trial commences are collateral to the indictment and not excluded by section 29(3); however judicial review of Crown Court bail refusals succeeds only exceptionally, and breach of bail conditions can reasonably justify continued custody even if reasons are minimally recorded.
legal_issues: Whether section 29(3) excluded judicial review of Crown Court bail decisions after arraignment
Whether insufficient reasons violated Article 5 or Thomassy v France
Whether breach of bail conditions alone justified refusal
Appropriate procedure and recording of reasons for bail applications

R v Manchester Crown Court, ex parte DPP [1994] Cr App R 461

notes: Permission refused on Taylor v Lawrence and second appeal; Back Land undervalue claim time-barred by earlier strike-out.

enrichment.short_title: Freeguard v RBS: second appeal on mortgage sale undervalue claim
key_facts: Mrs Freeguard claimed the Royal Bank of Scotland sold mortgaged Back Land and a ransom strip at undervalue after exercising its power of sale.
Deputy Master Cousins struck out the entire claim in August 2001; on appeal Mr Berry QC restored only the undervalue claim relating to the Strip with expert evidence.
Lightman J refused a Taylor v Lawrence application to reopen the strike-out; Master Bowles and HHJ Alton refused re-amendment to add Back Land undervalue and malicious falsehood claims.
The Strip trial was fixed for March 2005 when permission applications reached the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal against refusals of a Taylor v Lawrence reopening and of permission to re-amend particulars after partial restoration on appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Both permission applications refused; Taylor v Lawrence does not apply to first-instance decisions and no compelling reason existed for a second appeal on the Back Land amendments.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 52.17 cannot be used to challenge first-instance strike-out orders and the Court of Appeal has no jurisdiction to appeal a High Court refusal under that rule; second appeals under CPR 52.13(2) require an important point of principle or a truly compelling reason, not merely late pursuit of claims previously abandoned or unsupported by evidence.
legal_issues: Whether Taylor v Lawrence/CPR 52.17 applies to Deputy Master strike-out decisions
Whether the Court of Appeal can hear appeals from High Court CPR 52.17 refusals
Whether Back Land undervalue and malicious falsehood amendments should be permitted
Application of the compelling reason test for second appeals under Uphill
linked_authorities: Andrew Parker v Graham Hutchings [2004] EWCA Civ 254
Taylor v Lawrence [2002] EWCA Civ 90
Uphill v BRB (Residuary) Ltd [2005] EWCA Civ 60

notes: Permission to appeal refused; no error of law in IAT Article 8 decision on Iranian asylum seeker.

enrichment.short_title: Adelzadeh v SSHD: Article 8 permission appeal from IAT
key_facts: Mr Adelzadeh, an Iranian citizen, claimed asylum in October 2000; the adjudicator found his account lacking credibility and rejected asylum and Article 3 claims.
He formed a relationship with Ms Bruce who became pregnant; the adjudicator found family life existed but that she could accompany him to Iran.
On appeal to the IAT, Ms Bruce claimed employment with EDS on government contracts would expose her to death in Iran; the tribunal rejected that and said entry clearance could be sought from Tehran.
Fresh medical and persecution grounds raised before the Court of Appeal had not formed part of the IAT appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision on Article 8 grounds only.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no error of law identified in the tribunal's Article 8 analysis.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator and the IAT have properly assessed Article 8 family life and proportionality, including the option of the partner accompanying the appellant or obtaining entry clearance from abroad, the Court of Appeal will not grant permission absent an arguable point of law.
legal_issues: Whether Article 8 was infringed by requiring return to Iran despite family life in the UK
Whether Ms Bruce could reasonably be expected to live in Iran
Whether new medical and persecution arguments could be raised on permission to appeal
Proportionality of removal where family life was established

notes: AG reference; disguised loaded firearm sentence increased from 4 to 6 years after wrongful exceptional circumstances finding.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference No 5 of 2005: disguised firearm sentence
key_facts: A 20-year-old was seen cycling on a footpath in Stretford with a key-fob disguised .25mm gun loaded with two live rounds, body armour and thick gloves.
He pleaded guilty on the day of trial to possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life, possessing a disguised prohibited firearm and possessing ammunition without a certificate.
HHJ Mort imposed 4 years' detention concurrently, finding exceptional circumstances to avoid the 5-year minimum for the disguised firearm.
The offender was on bail for dangerous driving offences and in breach of a conditional discharge when arrested.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; sentences on counts 1 and 2 increased to 6 years' detention concurrently after double jeopardy adjustment (from 4 years).
enrichment.ratio: Low risk of re-offending in a pre-sentence report is not an exceptional circumstance for avoiding the mandatory minimum for a disguised firearm; carrying a loaded disguised weapon with intent to endanger life in a residential area while on bail warrants a substantially higher sentence than 4 years.
legal_issues: Whether the 4-year total sentence was unduly lenient for loaded disguised firearm offences
Whether exceptional circumstances existed to disapply the 5-year minimum under section 5(1A)
Appropriate sentence for possession with intent to endanger life in aggravating circumstances
Effect of double jeopardy on an Attorney General's reference

notes: Commercial waste tariff JR dismissed; Wandsworth could lawfully fix full-cost residual service charges.

enrichment.short_title: Western Riverside v Wandsworth: commercial waste collection JR
key_facts: Western Riverside Waste Authority challenged Wandsworth's August 2004 decision to fix high commercial waste tariffs and release Onyx from non-compete restrictions.
Wandsworth ended co-collection with household waste, sold its commercial portfolio to Onyx for £750,000, and set charges on a 10% residual customer base assumption.
Letters to businesses stated council charges would likely exceed private contractors and encouraged switching to Onyx or other licensed collectors.
The authority argued Wandsworth unlawfully thwarted its section 45(1)(b) duty and frustrated EPA 1990 policy by deterring commercial waste requests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review after permission granted on oral renewal, challenging Wandsworth's commercial waste tariff and Onyx release decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the tariff was a reasonable charge under section 45(4) and Wandsworth lawfully minimised its residual commercial collection service.
enrichment.ratio: A waste collection authority may fix commercial waste charges at full-cost recovery for an expected residual service without subsidising competition with private contractors; the EPA 1990 does not require WCAs to maximise waste delivered to WDAs or fix charges to retain commercial customers.
legal_issues: Whether Wandsworth's tariff was a reasonable charge under section 45(4)
Whether Wandsworth unlawfully denied or thwarted its duty to collect commercial waste on request
Whether the decision frustrated the policy and objects of the EPA 1990
Whether Wandsworth failed to have regard to the Mayor's Strategy and joint waste management strategy

notes: Indefinite Civil Proceedings Order under section 42 against habitual vexatious litigant Mrs Foden.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General v Foden: Civil Proceedings Order
key_facts: Mrs Foden brought 33 civil actions since 1989 arising mainly from a dispute over beneficial interest in her mother's Yelverton property, Glen View.
She repeatedly relitigated issues decided against her, sued solicitors and courts, and pursued judicial review of Western Circuit decisions.
Judge Overend and other judges described her as a compulsive litigant whose litigation consumed her mother's estate.
She failed to attend the section 42 hearing despite repeated adjournments based on medical certificates.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application under section 42 for an indefinite Civil Proceedings Order after interim restrictions since October 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Civil Proceedings Order made without limit of time; Mrs Foden may not institute or continue civil proceedings without High Court leave.
enrichment.ratio: Habitual and persistent litigation without reasonable ground, revisiting the same disputes after adverse decisions and collateral attacks on judges and solicitors, satisfies section 42; the court need not reopen the merits of underlying actions and may make an indefinite order where litigation has become compulsive and vexatious.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Foden habitually and persistently instituted vexatious proceedings without reasonable ground
Whether a Civil Proceedings Order should be indefinite
Whether adjournment was warranted on medical grounds
Application of the Barker hallmarks of section 42 litigation

notes: Exceptional bail JR success; Crown Court remand irrational where magistrates bail unbreached and self-harm risk unsupported.

enrichment.short_title: Allwin v Snaresbrook: exceptional judicial review granting bail
key_facts: The claimant was charged with affray after threatening self-harm with a lighter near a van containing petrol at a hostel exclusion dispute.
Magistrates remanded him initially but later granted bail to live with his parents after a psychiatric report showed no mental illness.
He rejected a prosecution offer of a bind over, pleaded not guilty on arraignment, and Circuit Judge Marney revoked bail fearing self-harm.
Police no longer opposed bail; there had been no breach of bail conditions while living at home.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission and substantive judicial review of Snaresbrook Crown Court bail refusal on arraignment.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted and claim succeeded exceptionally; bail directed on the same terms as the magistrates' order, remitted to the Crown Court for implementation.
enrichment.ratio: Judicial review of Crown Court bail refusals is available but sparingly; where magistrates granted bail without breach, police did not oppose, and the judge's self-harm concern lacked rational support on current facts, refusal falls outside Wednesbury reasonableness.
legal_issues: Whether section 29(3) barred judicial review of bail refusal after arraignment
Whether the Crown Court judge's self-harm rationale justified remand in custody
Correct Wednesbury standard for reviewing bail decisions
Procedural approach for urgent bail judicial review applications
